title: Imam al-Ash'ari
hookLine: a star pupil of the Mu'tazilah changes his mind, and keeps his tools

cards: Three brothers. One dies a faithful believer. One dies rejecting faith.
The third dies as a small child. Where does each one stand on the Day of Judgment? That puzzle, the later sources say, was put by a student in Basra to his teacher, al-Jubba'i, a Mu'tazili master.
The student was Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, who had studied Mu'tazili theology for years and could argue it with skill. By the time the conversation was over, the story goes, he had started to leave it.

teach.b: Here's the rest as it's told. The teacher answers: the believer in a high rank, the unbeliever punished, the child somewhere safe but lower, since he did no good works.
The student presses: what if the child says, Lord, why didn't You let me live long enough to earn more? The teacher says Allah knew it was better for him to die young.
Then what if the brother who rejected faith cries out, why didn't You take me as a child too? The teacher has no answer.
The story's point: insist that human reason can always explain what Allah's justice must do, and sooner or later you hit a question it can't answer.
Historians treat this story with caution, and other reasons for his turn are told too. But the turn itself is history.
Al-Ash'ari left the Mu'tazilah; some reports say he stood up in the mosque in Basra and announced it in public. What makes him matter is what he did next. He didn't throw away reason.

teach.h: HE KEEPS THE TOOLS OF KALAM.
teach.b: He took the tools of kalam, the careful arguments he'd learned, and turned them toward defending what the people of hadith already held: that the Qur'an is Allah's uncreated speech, that His attributes are real, that believers will see Him in the life to come.
Ahmad ibn Hanbal had answered with a request for a verse. Al-Ash'ari answered with the verse, and an argument to go with it.
Reason in the service of tradition: that's the line he drew, and others would follow it.

how: Sunni students of theology learn about al-Ash'ari as the scholar who left the Mu'tazilah and used kalam to defend the beliefs of the people of hadith, and the Ash'ari school is named after him.

o: a former Mu'tazili who used reason to defend traditional belief
a Mu'tazili teacher in Basra who had no answer for his student
the scholar who refused the caliph's test and was beaten for it

s: al-Ash'ari gave up reason when he left the Mu'tazilah
he kept the tools of kalam and used them to defend traditional belief.
al-Ash'ari had been a Mu'tazili himself
he studied under al-Jubba'i before he changed his mind.
historians accept the three brothers story without question
it comes from later sources and is treated with caution.

games.q: you're al-Ash'ari. your teacher can't answer your question about the three brothers. what do you do?
o: leave the Mu'tazilah, and use reason to defend traditional belief.
keep quiet and stay in the circle.
games.why: he left, by some reports announcing it in the Basra mosque, and turned the tools of kalam toward the beliefs of the people of hadith.

practice: Bring to mind something you once held firmly and see differently now, a view, a habit, a person you misjudged, and notice what changed it.

Look at your old self without contempt, and, like al-Ash'ari, who kept his years of study and turned them, ask what from the old view is worth keeping. If you pray, you can thank Allah for whatever led you on.

wordCard.voice: Imam al-Ash'ari. Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari: a former Mu'tazili who used reason to defend traditional belief. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Ash'ari, a name from his tribe, the Ash'ar.

carryVoice: Your line: reason for tradition. He changed his mind and kept his tools. Same time tomorrow.
